**Contains Duplicate** · Easy

You get an array of integers `nums`. Return `true` if at least one value appears two or more times anywhere in the array, and `false` if every value is distinct.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵
- −10⁹ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3,1]` → Output: `true` (1 sits at index 0 and index 3)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3,4]` → Output: `false` (all four values differ)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [1,1,1,3,3,4,3,2,4,2]` → Output: `true`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/duplicate-integer) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate/)

**Valid Anagram** · Easy

You get two strings `s` and `t`. Return `true` if `t` uses exactly the same letters as `s`, each one the same number of times, just possibly in a different order. Otherwise return `false`.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ s.length, t.length ≤ 5 · 10⁴
- both strings contain only lowercase English letters

**Example 1**
Input: `s = "anagram", t = "nagaram"` → Output: `true` (both have three a's and one each of n, g, r, m)

**Example 2**
Input: `s = "rat", t = "car"` → Output: `false` (`t` has a `c` and no `t`)

**Example 3**
Input: `s = "aacc", t = "ccac"` → Output: `false` (same letters, different counts)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/is-anagram) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-anagram/)

**Two Sum** · Easy

You get an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`. Find two **different positions** `i` and `j` whose values add up to `target`, and return `[i, j]`. Exactly one such pair exists, and a single element can't be used twice. Any order of the two indices is accepted.

**Constraints**
- 2 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁴
- −10⁹ ≤ nums[i], target ≤ 10⁹
- exactly one valid answer exists

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [2,7,11,15], target = 9` → Output: `[0,1]` (2 + 7 = 9)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [3,2,4], target = 6` → Output: `[1,2]` (2 + 4; index 0 can't pair with itself)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [3,3], target = 6` → Output: `[0,1]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/two-integer-sum) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/)

**Group Anagrams** · Medium

You get a list of strings `strs`. Put the strings into groups so that two strings share a group exactly when they are anagrams of each other (same letters, same counts). Return the groups as a list of lists. The order of the groups and the order inside each group don't matter.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ strs.length ≤ 10⁴
- 0 ≤ strs[i].length ≤ 100
- strings contain only lowercase English letters

**Example 1**
Input: `strs = ["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"]`
Output: `[["bat"],["nat","tan"],["ate","eat","tea"]]`
`eat`, `tea` and `ate` all use one e, one a and one t. `tan` and `nat` match each other. `bat` has no partner.

**Example 2**
Input: `strs = [""]` → Output: `[[""]]` (the empty string is its own group)

**Example 3**
Input: `strs = ["a"]` → Output: `[["a"]]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/anagram-groups) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/group-anagrams/)

**Top K Frequent Elements** · Medium

You get an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Return the `k` values that occur most often in `nums`, in any order. The input is guaranteed to make the answer unique (there is no tie at the cut-off).

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵
- −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴
- 1 ≤ k ≤ number of distinct values
- the answer is unique
- aim for better than O(n log n)

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [1,1,1,2,2,3], k = 2` → Output: `[1,2]` (1 appears 3 times, 2 appears twice, 3 once)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [1], k = 1` → Output: `[1]`

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [4,4,-1,-1,-1,7], k = 1` → Output: `[-1]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/top-k-elements-in-list) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/)

**Encode and Decode Strings** · Medium

Design two methods. `encode` turns a list of strings into **one** string. `decode` takes that string and must rebuild exactly the original list: same strings, same order, including empty strings. The strings may contain any characters, including whatever separator you might want to use, so plain joining on a delimiter isn't safe.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ strs.length ≤ 100
- 0 ≤ strs[i].length ≤ 200
- strs[i] may contain any of the 256 ASCII characters
- `decode(encode(strs))` must equal `strs`

**Example 1**
Input: `["neet","code","love","you"]` → `decode(encode(...))` = `["neet","code","love","you"]`

**Example 2**
Input: `["we","say",":","yes"]` → round-trips unchanged. One string is just `":"`, so `":"` can't be the separator.

**Example 3**
Input: `["","#","12#ab"]` → round-trips unchanged. Empty strings and strings that look like your own framing must survive.

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/string-encode-and-decode) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/encode-and-decode-strings/) (Premium)

**Product of Array Except Self** · Medium

You get an integer array `nums`. Build an array `answer` of the same length where `answer[i]` is the product of every element of `nums` **except** `nums[i]`. Don't use division, and aim for O(n) time. Every such product fits in a 32-bit integer.

**Constraints**
- 2 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵
- −30 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 30
- every prefix and suffix product fits in a 32-bit int

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [1,2,3,4]` → Output: `[24,12,8,6]` (e.g. index 1: 1·3·4 = 12)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [-1,1,0,-3,3]` → Output: `[0,0,9,0,0]` (only index 2, the zero, skips the zero: −1·1·−3·3 = 9)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [2,3]` → Output: `[3,2]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/products-of-array-discluding-self) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/product-of-array-except-self/)

**Valid Sudoku** · Medium

You get a 9 × 9 Sudoku board, partly filled. Each cell holds a digit `"1"`–`"9"` or `"."` for empty. Decide whether the **filled cells so far** break any rule:
- no digit repeats within a row,
- no digit repeats within a column,
- no digit repeats within any of the nine 3 × 3 boxes.

You don't have to check whether the puzzle can actually be solved. Only the cells already placed count.

**Constraints**
- `board` is 9 × 9
- each cell is a digit `1`–`9` or `.`

**Example 1**

```grid
5 3 . . 7 . . . .
6 . . 1 9 5 . . .
. 9 8 . . . . 6 .
8 . . . 6 . . . 3
4 . . 8 . 3 . . 1
7 . . . 2 . . . 6
. 6 . . . . 2 8 .
. . . 4 1 9 . . 5
. . . . 8 . . 7 9
caption: valid: no clashes in any row, column or box
```

Input: the board above → Output: `true`

**Example 2**

```grid
8! 3 . . 7 . . . .
6 . . 1 9 5 . . .
. 9 8! . . . . 6 .
8! . . . 6 . . . 3
4 . . 8 . 3 . . 1
7 . . . 2 . . . 6
. 6 . . . . 2 8 .
. . . 4 1 9 . . 5
. . . . 8 . . 7 9
caption: invalid: the 8 at top-left clashes with column 0 and its box
```

Input: same board, but the top-left `5` is replaced by `8` → Output: `false`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/valid-sudoku) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-sudoku/)

**Longest Consecutive Sequence** · Medium

You get an unsorted integer array `nums`. Find the length of the longest run of integers `x, x+1, x+2, …` whose values **all appear somewhere** in `nums`. Positions don't matter, only which values are present, and duplicates count once. Aim for O(n) time.

**Constraints**
- 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵
- −10⁹ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [100,4,200,1,3,2]` → Output: `4` (the values 1, 2, 3, 4 are all present)

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [0,3,7,2,5,8,4,6,0,1]` → Output: `9` (0 through 8; the second 0 doesn't add length)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = []` → Output: `0`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/longest-consecutive-sequence) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-consecutive-sequence/)

**Valid Palindrome** · Easy

You get a string `s`. Lowercase every letter and throw away every character that isn't a letter or a digit. Return `true` if what's left reads the same forwards and backwards, otherwise `false`. A string with nothing left counts as a palindrome.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 2 · 10⁵
- `s` consists of printable ASCII characters

**Example 1**
Input: `s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"` → Output: `true` (cleaned: `amanaplanacanalpanama`)

**Example 2**
Input: `s = "race a car"` → Output: `false` (cleaned: `raceacar`, reversed `racaecar`)

**Example 3**
Input: `s = " "` → Output: `true` (nothing alphanumeric is left, and an empty string is a palindrome)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/is-palindrome) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-palindrome/)

**Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted** · Medium

You get an integer array `numbers` sorted in non-decreasing order and an integer `target`. Exactly one pair of different positions adds up to `target`. Return those positions as **1-based** indices `[index1, index2]` with `index1 < index2`. Use only O(1) extra space.

**Constraints**
- 2 ≤ numbers.length ≤ 3 · 10⁴
- −1000 ≤ numbers[i], target ≤ 1000
- `numbers` is sorted ascending; exactly one solution exists

**Example 1**
Input: `numbers = [2,7,11,15], target = 9` → Output: `[1,2]` (2 + 7, at 1-based positions 1 and 2)

**Example 2**
Input: `numbers = [2,3,4], target = 6` → Output: `[1,3]` (2 + 4)

**Example 3**
Input: `numbers = [-1,0], target = -1` → Output: `[1,2]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/two-integer-sum-ii) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted/)

**3Sum** · Medium

You get an integer array `nums`. Find every distinct triplet of values `[a, b, c]`, taken from three different positions, with `a + b + c = 0`. Two triplets with the same values count once, even if they come from different positions. Return the triplets in any order.

**Constraints**
- 3 ≤ nums.length ≤ 3000
- −10⁵ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵

**Example 1**
Input: `nums = [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4]` → Output: `[[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]]`
The triplet −1, 0, 1 can be built from either −1, but it's listed only once.

**Example 2**
Input: `nums = [0,1,1]` → Output: `[]` (no three values sum to 0)

**Example 3**
Input: `nums = [0,0,0]` → Output: `[[0,0,0]]`

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/three-integer-sum) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/3sum/)

**Container With Most Water** · Medium

You get an array `height` where `height[i]` is the height of a vertical wall standing at x = i. Choose two walls. Together with the x-axis they form a container that holds `min(height[i], height[j]) × (j − i)` units of water. Return the most water any pair of walls can hold. Walls can't be tilted.

**Constraints**
- 2 ≤ height.length ≤ 10⁵
- 0 ≤ height[i] ≤ 10⁴

**Example 1**
Input: `height = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]` → Output: `49`
The walls at x = 1 (height 8) and x = 8 (height 7): min(8, 7) × 7 = 49.

**Example 2**
Input: `height = [1,1]` → Output: `1`

**Example 3**
Input: `height = [4,3,2,1,4]` → Output: `16` (the two 4s, 4 apart)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/max-water-container) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/container-with-most-water/)

**Trapping Rain Water** · Hard

You get an array `height` of non-negative integers. Each entry is a bar of width 1 in an elevation map. After it rains, water settles in the dips between bars. Return the total units of water trapped. Water at a column rises to the lower of the tallest bar on its left and the tallest bar on its right, and anything above that spills off.

**Constraints**
- 1 ≤ height.length ≤ 2 · 10⁴
- 0 ≤ height[i] ≤ 10⁵

**Example 1**

```grid
· · · · · · · #* · · · ·
· · · #* ~+ ~+ ~+ #* #* ~+ #* ·
· #* ~+ #* #* ~+ #* #* #* #* #* #*
0 1 0 2 1 0 1 3 2 1 2 1
caption: bars (#, blue) and trapped water (~, green); bottom row = heights
```

Input: `height = [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1]`
Output: `6`
There are six green cells: one in the first dip, four in the middle basin, one in the right dip.

**Example 2**
Input: `height = [4,2,0,3,2,5]` → Output: `9`

**Example 3**
Input: `height = [3,2,1]` → Output: `0` (the bars only go down, so the water runs off the right side)

[NeetCode](https://neetcode.io/problems/trapping-rain-water) · [LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/trapping-rain-water/)
